title: Interesting video from 2013, when John Carmack gets asked if an individual is ever going to be able to produce a game of AAA quality. We're definitely not there yet, but I would like to hear how his answer would change in 2026.

comments.author: Upstairs_Weird_760
comments.body:
I think we’re closer than this post gives us credit for, but “AAA quality” is doing a lot of work here.  
One person can already build systems that would have required a small team not that long ago. I’m building a first-person movement roguelite with wall running, sliding, air movement, combat systems, enemy AI, procedural level pieces, etc., and AI has massively increased what I can realistically attempt by myself.  
But AI hasn’t eliminated the hard part. It’s mostly changed the bottleneck. Instead of needing to personally write every system, I spend a ridiculous amount of time defining architecture, reviewing implementations, debugging interactions between systems, reverting bad changes, managing context, and deciding what the game should actually be.  
And then there’s animation, art direction, modeling, VFX, sound, level design, optimization, QA, marketing… all the stuff that makes something actually *feel* AAA rather than just having a lot of features.  
So can one person make something with AAA-looking pieces now? Absolutely. Can one person make the equivalent of a modern AAA game end-to-end? I don’t think we’re there. AI is multiplying the developer, not magically turning one developer into a 300-person studio.

comments.author: i_rate_slop
comments.body:
I'd say we're a year or so away from very, very good AAA quality content pipelines that can be operated by one or a small handful of people. Maybe two or three if you want to be pessimistic.

I think what AAA means has to change. It's not going to mean visual quality anymore, but rather raw scope where armies of people make sense.

With the advent of AI as it is today, I expect EA to produce The Sims 5 on a level we've never seen before. I mean, we all know EA won't adapt that fast, but it's what I expect from AAA now. The next Sims game better be massive in content and the raw technology behind the simulation itself should be on another level. If an indie developer can make The Sims now, which they can, I expect AAA to push technical boundaries the extreme.

comments.author: kUkara4
comments.body:
Still not there, because the definition of what AAA means keeps updating and the bar of AAA keeps rising. And it will increase proportionally with time.

At best an individual is able to produce a very short demo that maybe can compare to AAA. A studio size needed, however, keeps shrinking down. Except it's more of a sin curve, since AAA studios in the early days used to be pretty small, then they ballooned, and now smaller studios can make AAA games again.

Here are a few AAA things that appeared more recently that are very hard for an individual to replicate:
1. Acting, voice acting, facial acting, having actors.
2. Sound design and sound tracks.
3. Memorable graphic design or art direction.
The list can go on.

If anyone thinks that Astra or Opus are anywhere close to helping any individual make a AAA game, they are delusional and should read about the Dunning-Kruger effect.

comments.author: Excellent-Basket-825

What you guys don't understand is that if tools improve the demands are also shifting. Creating "fun" has not become easier, creating better graphics and systems around etc. for sure.

That'll simply shift what gamers expect as a bare minimum. So what triple AAA is, is shifting. That's why a game from the 90s today that was considered AAA would never make the same amount of money, regardless of any nostalgia.
